questions.question: What was the total number of Alvar saints in the Bhakti movement tradition?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**12**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Alvar saints** were a group of **12 Tamil poet-saints** who were devoted to the worship of the Hindu god Vishnu.
 
• Their devotional hymns, composed between the 6th and 9th centuries CE, are collectively known as the **Nalayira Divya Prabandham**, consisting of 4,000 verses.
 
• The Alvars played a crucial role in the **Bhakti movement**, promoting devotion (bhakti) to Vishnu as a personal and direct form of worship.
 
• Prominent Alvar saints include **Andal** (the only female Alvar), **Nammalvar**, and **Thirumangai Alvar**, among others.
 
• The Alvars' teachings emphasized equality and devotion, rejecting social hierarchies and fostering a sense of universal brotherhood in spirituality.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Role of Alvars in Bhakti Movement:**

 
 
• The Bhakti movement emerged as a significant reformist movement in medieval India, emphasizing individual devotion over ritualistic practices.
 
• The Alvars contributed to the spread of the Bhakti ideals in South India, especially in Tamil Nadu, through their accessible and emotive hymns.
 
• Their compositions were written in Tamil, making spiritual teachings accessible to the common people.
 
 
 
• **Notable Alvars and Their Contributions:**
 
 
• **Nammalvar:** Considered the greatest of the Alvars, he composed works like *Tiruvaimozhi*, expressing intense devotion and love for Vishnu.
 
• **Andal:** The only female Alvar, her hymns, particularly the *Tiruppavai*, are still recited in temples and during festivals.
 
• **Periyalvar:** Known for his hymns celebrating the childhood of Lord Krishna.
 
 
 
• **Key Themes in Alvar Hymns:**
 
 
• Devotion to Vishnu as the supreme deity.
 
• Rejection of caste-based discrimination and promotion of spiritual equality.
 
• Focus on surrender (Prapatti) as the path to salvation.
 
 
 
• **Legacy of Alvars:**
 
 
• The hymns of the Alvars were collected and compiled by Nathamuni in the 10th century into the **Nalayira Divya Prabandham**.
 
• The Alvars' contributions significantly shaped the Sri Vaishnavism tradition, which later influenced the teachings of philosophers like **Ramanuja**.
 
• Their works continue to inspire festivals, temple rituals, and cultural practices in South India.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Terminology:**

 
 
• **Alvar:** Derived from the Tamil word "Azhwar," meaning "one who is immersed" in devotion.
 
• **Bhakti:** Refers to devotion and love for a personal god, central to the teachings of the Alvars.
 
 
 
• **Temples Associated with Alvars:**
 
 
• The Alvars are closely associated with the **108 Divya Desams** (sacred Vishnu temples) mentioned in their hymns.
 
• These temples, spread across India, are significant pilgrimage sites for devotees of Vishnu.
 
 
 
• **Modern Relevance:**
 
 
• The Alvars' teachings continue to resonate with followers of Vaishnavism, emphasizing devotion, compassion, and equality.
 
• Their hymns are integral to religious practices and cultural traditions in South India.

questions.question: The nickname "Flying Sikh" is associated with which Indian athlete?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Milkha Singh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Milkha Singh**, popularly known as the **"Flying Sikh,"** was one of India's most celebrated athletes and a national sports icon.
 
• He earned the nickname "Flying Sikh" after his outstanding performance in the **1960 Rome Olympics** and his incredible speed and stamina in track events.
 
• Milkha Singh was a four-time **Asian Games gold medalist** and represented India in the **1956, 1960, and 1964 Olympics**.
 
• His most notable performance came during the **1960 Rome Olympics**, where he finished fourth in the 400 meters final, narrowly missing a medal.
 
• Milkha Singh's story of resilience and determination, particularly in overcoming the traumas of the Partition of India, has inspired millions of Indians and was immortalized in the Bollywood biopic **"Bhaag Milkha Bhaag"** released in 2013.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Milkha Singh's Achievements:**

 
 
• He won the **gold medal** in the 1958 Commonwealth Games, becoming the first Indian male athlete to achieve this feat.
 
• He clinched **four gold medals** in the Asian Games: two in the **1958 Games (200m and 400m)** and two in the **1962 Games (400m and 4x400m relay)**.
 
 
 
• **Nickname Origin:**
 
 
• The title **"Flying Sikh"** was reportedly given to him by the then President of Pakistan, **General Ayub Khan**, after Milkha Singh's victory in a race against Pakistan's **Abdul Khaliq** in 1960.
 
 
 
• **Early Life:**
 
 
• Milkha Singh was born on **20 November 1929**, in Govindpura, a village now in Pakistan.
 
• He witnessed the horrors of the **Partition of India**, during which he lost his parents and several family members.
 
• He joined the Indian Army in **1951**, which marked the beginning of his career in athletics.
 
 
 
• **Legacy:**
 
 
• Milkha Singh passed away on **18 June 2021**, but his legacy continues to inspire budding athletes in India and abroad.
 
• His autobiography, **"The Race of My Life,"** co-written with his daughter, provides insights into his journey of struggle and success.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Avinash Sable:**

 
 
• An Indian track and field athlete specializing in **3000m steeplechase**.
 
• He holds the **national record** in steeplechase and represented India in **multiple international events**.
 
 
 
• **Vikas Gowda:**
 
 
• An Indian **discus thrower** and shot putter who has won medals at **Commonwealth Games** and **Asian Games**.
 
• He was the first Indian male athlete to win a gold medal in discus throw at the **2014 Commonwealth Games**.
 
 
 
• **Harbhajan Singh:**
 
 
• A renowned Indian **cricketer** who played as an off-spinner in the Indian cricket team.
 
• He is one of the most successful bowlers in Indian cricket history and played a pivotal role in India's victory in the **2007 ICC T20 World Cup** and **2011 ICC Cricket World Cup**.

questions.question: In May 2025, who has been given one-year extension as the Chairman of the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) and Secretary of the Department of Defence Research and Development (DDR&D) from India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Dr. Samir V. Kamat**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **Dr. Samir V. Kamat** has been given a **one-year extension** as the Chairman of the **Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO)** and Secretary of the **Department of Defence Research and Development (DDR&D)** in **May 2025**.

• Dr. Kamat is a distinguished scientist known for his contributions to **materials engineering** and advanced technologies in defense applications.

• He initially assumed the position of DRDO Chairman in **August 2022**, succeeding Dr. G. Satheesh Reddy.

• DRDO plays a vital role in India’s defense sector, focusing on **research and development** of advanced technologies for military applications, including missiles, radar systems, and combat aircraft.

• The extension ensures continuity in leadership for ongoing critical defense projects and strengthens India's defense capabilities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO):**

• DRDO is headquartered in **New Delhi** and functions under the Ministry of Defence, Government of India.

• Founded in **1958**, DRDO focuses on developing military technologies such as **missiles, avionics, electronics, and combat systems**.

• It operates through a network of over **50 laboratories** and research centers across India.

• DRDO's notable projects include the development of the **Agni missile series**, **BrahMos missile**, and the **Tejas Light Combat Aircraft**.

• **Dr. Samir V. Kamat:**

• Dr. Kamat specializes in **materials science** and has contributed significantly to the development of advanced **metals and alloys** for defense technologies.

• He completed his doctoral studies at the **Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bengaluru**.

• Before becoming DRDO Chairman, he served as the Director General of the **Naval Systems and Materials Division** at DRDO.

• **Recent Developments:**

• Under Dr. Kamat's leadership, DRDO has intensified efforts towards achieving **self-reliance** in defense manufacturing and promoting the **Make in India** initiative.

• Key projects include indigenization of military equipment and collaboration with private defense companies.

• **Importance of Leadership in DRDO:**

• The Chairman plays a pivotal role in steering research priorities, ensuring project deadlines, and collaborating with international defense organizations.

• Leadership continuity is crucial for the success of long-term strategic programs such as the **Integrated Guided Missile Development Program (IGMDP)**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Extension of DRDO Leadership:** Leadership extensions are often granted to ensure continuity in critical defense projects that require consistent oversight and strategic direction.

• **DRDO Achievements:** DRDO has developed cutting-edge technologies, including the **Ballistic Missile Defense System** and **Advanced Towed Artillery Gun Systems**.

• **India's Defense Goals:** India aims to be a global leader in defense production, reducing dependency on foreign imports and enhancing **indigenous capabilities**.

questions.question: In the Union Budget 2025-26, a Maritime Development Fund of Rs. _________ crore over 10 years has been announced.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**25000 crore**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• The **Maritime Development Fund** was announced in the **Union Budget 2025-26** with a fund allocation of **Rs. 25,000 crore** to be utilized over a period of 10 years. 
• The purpose of this fund is to enhance the development of the maritime sector, which includes **ports, shipping, and waterways infrastructure** in India. 
• This fund aims to support initiatives such as **modernization of ports**, expansion of shipping facilities, and development of inland waterways to improve logistics efficiency. 
• The maritime sector is critical for India's economy as it handles about **95% of the country's trade by volume** and contributes significantly to reducing transportation costs. 
• The creation of the Maritime Development Fund aligns with the government's vision of transforming India into a global maritime hub under the **Sagarmala Programme**. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __

• India has a coastline of about **7,517 kilometers**, making the maritime sector essential for trade and logistics. 
• The sector supports **employment generation**, boosts exports, and strengthens international trade partnerships. 
• Ports like **Mumbai, Chennai, and Kolkata** are key contributors to India's export-import activities. 
• **Sagarmala Programme:** 
• This flagship initiative was launched by the Government of India to enhance port-led development. 
• It focuses on port modernization, connectivity improvement, **port-linked industrialization**, and coastal community development. 
• The Sagarmala Programme aims to reduce logistics costs for both domestic and EXIM (Export-Import) cargo. 
• **Inland Waterways Development:** 
• India has about **14,500 kilometers** of navigable inland waterways. 
• The government has been promoting the use of waterways for cargo transportation through projects like **National Waterway-1 (NW-1)** on the Ganga River. 
• This mode of transport is environmentally friendly and cost-effective compared to road and rail transportation. 
• **Global Maritime Trends:** 
• Many countries are investing in **green shipping**, automation, and digitalization of ports to enhance efficiency and sustainability. 
• India's Maritime Development Fund aligns with these global trends by promoting **modern infrastructure** and eco-friendly practices. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Maritime India Vision 2030:** 
• This document outlines the strategic roadmap for India's maritime sector till 2030. 
• It includes plans for port capacity expansion, digital transformation, and integration of sustainable practices. 
• The Maritime Development Fund will play a crucial role in achieving the goals set under this vision. 
• **Economic Impact:** 
• Investments in the maritime sector can significantly contribute to India's **GDP growth**. 
• Efficient ports and waterways reduce logistics costs, making Indian exports more competitive globally. 
• This fund supports the government's aim to achieve a **$5 trillion economy**. </ul

questions.question: NTPC, India's largest power producer, inaugurated the world's first CO2-to-methanol conversion plant at its ________ facility.
questions.solution:

__

• **NTPC (National Thermal Power Corporation)**, India's largest power producer, inaugurated the world's first **CO2-to-methanol conversion plant** at its **Vindhyachal Super Thermal Power Station** in **Madhya Pradesh**.

• The Vindhyachal plant is the largest power station in India, with a total installed capacity of **4,760 MW**.

• The CO2-to-methanol conversion technology aims to reduce **carbon emissions** by capturing carbon dioxide and converting it into methanol, a valuable chemical used in various industries.

• The NTPC's initiative supports India's commitment to **reducing greenhouse gas emissions** under the Paris Agreement and achieving its carbon-neutral goals.

• The project is a step towards promoting **clean energy** and achieving a circular carbon economy by utilizing the by-products of power generation efficiently.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Vindhyachal Super Thermal Power Station:**

• Located in **Singrauli district, Madhya Pradesh**, this plant is the largest thermal power plant in India.

• It is operated by **NTPC** and has a total installed capacity of **4,760 MW** through its coal-fired units.

• It plays a crucial role in meeting the energy demands of India by contributing significantly to the power grid.

• **CO2-to-Methanol Conversion Technology:**

• This innovative technology captures carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from industrial processes and converts them into methanol.

• **Methanol** is a versatile chemical used as a fuel, solvent, and in the production of plastics and other materials.

• The process helps reduce **carbon emissions**, contributing to cleaner energy solutions and environmental sustainability.

• **NTPC's Role in India's Energy Sector:**

• NTPC is India's largest power utility, with an installed capacity exceeding **73 GW** (as of 2023).

• It is actively working on renewable energy projects, including **solar, wind, and hydrogen**, to diversify its energy portfolio.

• The company is contributing to India's **energy transition goals** by adopting innovative technologies and reducing dependency on fossil fuels.

• **India's Carbon Reduction Goals:**

• Under the **Paris Agreement**, India has committed to reducing its carbon intensity by **33-35%** by 2030, compared to 2005 levels.

• The country aims to achieve **net-zero carbon emissions** by 2070, focusing on renewable energy, energy efficiency, and carbon capture technologies.

• Initiatives like the CO2-to-methanol plant align with these goals and promote sustainable industrial practices.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **About Methanol:**

• **Methanol** is a simple alcohol with the chemical formula **CH3OH**.

• It is used as a fuel in vehicles, a solvent in various industries, and a raw material in chemical manufacturing.

• Methanol is considered a cleaner alternative to fossil fuels due to its lower carbon emissions.

• **Carbon Capture and Utilization (CCU):**

• CCU involves capturing carbon dioxide from industrial emissions and repurposing it for useful applications, such as producing fuels, chemicals, or building materials.

• It is a key technology in combating climate change and promoting sustainable industrial practices.

• **NTPC's Environmental Initiatives:**

• NTPC has been actively working on projects like **flue gas desulfurization (FGD)**, renewable energy, and hydrogen blending in pipelines to reduce its environmental footprint.

• The company is also involved in **afforestation projects** and promoting energy-efficient technologies.

questions.question: Who is the author of the book 'Shalimar The Clown'?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Salman Rushdie**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Salman Rushdie** is the author of the acclaimed novel **'Shalimar The Clown'**, which was published in **2005**.
 
• The book is a multifaceted story that spans continents, focusing on themes of **love, betrayal, revenge, and political turmoil**.
 
• It is set in the fictional village of **Pachigam in Kashmir** and explores the socio-political conflicts in the region, blending historical events with fiction.
 
• 'Shalimar The Clown' was shortlisted for several prestigious awards, including the **Whitbread Book Awards** and the **Commonwealth Writers' Prize**.
 
• Salman Rushdie, born in **1947 in Mumbai, India**, is a celebrated British-Indian novelist and essayist known for his use of magical realism and historical narrative.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Salman Rushdie's Background:**

 
 
• Salman Rushdie's first novel, **'Grimus'**, was published in **1975**, but he gained international fame with his second novel, **'Midnight's Children'**, which won the **Booker Prize in 1981**.
 
• He is renowned for his distinctive narrative style, which often combines magical realism with historical and political themes.
 
 
 
• **'Shalimar The Clown': Key Themes and Plot:**
 
 
• The novel explores the **impact of terrorism** and the **loss of cultural harmony** in Kashmir.
 
• The protagonist, Shalimar, transforms from a traditional Kashmiri performer into a **vengeful assassin** following a series of personal and political betrayals.
 
• It delves into the **ethnic and religious strife** in Kashmir, providing a nuanced portrayal of its socio-political complexities.
 
 
 
• **Other Works by Salman Rushdie:**
 
 
• **'The Satanic Verses'** (1988): One of his most controversial works, which led to a fatwa being issued against him by Iran's Ayatollah Khomeini.
 
• **'Midnight's Children'** (1981): A landmark novel that examines India's post-independence history through magical realism.
 
• **'The Moor's Last Sigh'** (1995): A family saga that spans several generations, dealing with themes of art, politics, and betrayal.
 
 
 
• **Recognition and Awards:**
 
 
• Salman Rushdie has received numerous accolades, including being knighted in **2007** for his contributions to literature.
 
• He was awarded the **Booker of Bookers** in 1993 and 2008 for **'Midnight's Children'**, recognizing it as the best Booker Prize-winning novel in the award's history.
 
 
 
• **Other Authors Mentioned in the Question:**
 
 
• **Anita Desai:** Known for works like **'Clear Light of Day'** and **'In Custody'**, focusing on themes of personal and cultural identity.
 
• **Shiva Naipaul:** The younger brother of Nobel laureate V.S. Naipaul, recognized for books like **'Fireflies'** and **'North of South'**.
 
• **Rohinton Mistry:** Famous for novels such as **'A Fine Balance'** and **'Family Matters'**, depicting the lives of India's Parsi community.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Kashmir as a Theme:**

 
 
• The novel provides an in-depth exploration of the cultural and political history of **Kashmir**, highlighting its transition from a peaceful region to one marked by violence and division.
 
• Through its characters and setting, the book illustrates the **human cost of political conflict** and the erosion of cultural harmony.
 
 
 
• **Magical Realism in Salman Rushdie's Works:**
 
 
• Rushdie is known for weaving **magical realism** into his narratives, blending fantastical elements with real-world events.
 
• In **'Shalimar The Clown'**, the magical realism enhances the storytelling, making it both poetic and poignant.

questions.question: The Indus Valley people used standardized __________ as a building material.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**burnt mud-bricks**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Indus Valley Civilization**, also known as the Harappan Civilization, flourished around **2500 BCE to 1900 BCE** in present-day India and Pakistan.
 
• The use of **burnt mud-bricks** as a standardized building material was one of the most remarkable features of the civilization. This indicates their advanced knowledge of construction techniques and urban planning.
 
• The bricks were made by firing clay in kilns at high temperatures, which made them durable and resistant to weathering, ensuring the longevity of their structures.
 
• The uniformity in the size and shape of the bricks reflects a well-organized system of production and standardization, suggesting the existence of centralized authority or governance.
 
• Structures like houses, granaries, drainage systems, and public baths in cities such as **Mohenjo-daro** and **Harappa** were constructed using these bricks, showcasing the civilization's focus on hygiene and urban organization.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Indus Valley Civilization:**

 
 
• This was one of the world's first major urban civilizations, comparable to Mesopotamia and Ancient Egypt.
 
• The civilization was spread over modern-day **Pakistan, northwest India, and parts of Afghanistan.**
 
• Famous cities include **Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Lothal, Dholavira**, and **Kalibangan**.
 
 
 
• **Construction Techniques:**
 
 
• The bricks were made using a precise ratio of clay and sand, ensuring durability and uniformity.
 
• Bricks were fired in kilns at temperatures exceeding **800°C**, which made them water-resistant and long-lasting.
 
• The construction employed an interlocking system to enhance the stability of walls.
 
 
 
• **Urban Planning:**
 
 
• Indus cities were meticulously planned with a grid-like layout, wide roads, and sophisticated drainage systems.
 
• Buildings were often multi-storied and had flat roofs made using wooden beams and mud plaster.
 
• The use of burnt bricks in drainage systems highlights the importance given to sanitation and hygiene.
 
 
 
• **Other Building Materials:**
 
 
• While burnt mud-bricks were the primary material, sun-dried bricks were also used for less important structures.
 
• Stone was occasionally used, especially in regions where it was readily available, but it was not as common as bricks.
 
• Timber was used for door frames, roofs, and other structural supports.
 
 
 
• **Innovations:**
 
 
• The Harappans were pioneers in using standard weights and measures, which contributed to the uniformity in brick sizes.
 
• They also developed sophisticated water management systems, including wells, reservoirs, and public baths, such as the famous Great Bath of Mohenjo-daro.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Burnt Mud-Bricks:**

 
 
• These were used extensively in constructing houses, granaries, and public infrastructure.

questions.question: In the context of Indian satellite launch vehicle, what does "G" stands for in GSLV?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Geosynchronous**__.

 __ 
• **GSLV stands for Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle.** The letter "G" in GSLV represents "Geosynchronous," referring to the type of orbit that the launch vehicle is designed to achieve. 
• A **Geosynchronous orbit** is an orbit where the satellite's orbital period matches Earth's rotational period, allowing the satellite to appear stationary relative to the Earth's surface. 
• The GSLV is developed by the **Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)** for launching heavier payloads into geosynchronous or geostationary transfer orbits. 
• The GSLV is capable of launching satellites weighing up to **5,000 kg** into low Earth orbit and approximately **2,500 kg** into geostationary transfer orbit. 
• GSLV is equipped with an indigenously developed **Cryogenic Upper Stage (CUS)**, which provides enhanced performance during the final stage of flight. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Geosynchronous Orbit:** 
• A satellite in a **Geosynchronous orbit** completes one orbit around Earth in the same time it takes Earth to rotate once (approximately 24 hours). 
• Satellites in this orbit are typically used for **communication, broadcasting, and weather monitoring**. 
• A subset of geosynchronous orbit is the **Geostationary orbit**, where the satellite remains fixed at one position above the Earth's equator. 
• **Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO):** 
• **ISRO** is India's national space agency headquartered in Bengaluru. 
• It was established in **1969** and operates under the Department of Space, Government of India. 
• ISRO is responsible for launching satellites, exploring space, and providing technological advancements in fields like **telecommunication, navigation, and remote sensing**. 
• **GSLV Variants:** 
• GSLV has undergone several advancements, leading to multiple variants like **GSLV Mk I, Mk II, and Mk III**. 
• **GSLV Mk III** is India's most powerful rocket, capable of launching heavier satellites and is used for missions like **Chandrayaan-2**. 
• **Applications of GSLV:** 
• Launching communication satellites like **GSAT series** for telecommunication and internet services. 
• Supporting space exploration missions, including **Chandrayaan** and future interplanetary missions. 
• Expanding India's presence in **commercial satellite launches**, boosting economic and technological growth. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Cryogenic Technology:** 
• GSLV's cryogenic upper stage uses **liquid hydrogen** and **liquid oxygen** as propellants, providing higher thrust compared to conventional fuels. 
• India developed indigenous cryogenic technology after overcoming challenges due to **international sanctions** in the 1990s. 
• **Global Context:** 
• India's GSLV competes with international space agencies like NASA, Roscosmos, and ESA in launching satellites for global clients. 
• Successful GSLV missions enhance India's reputation in **space technology and commercial satellite launching**. </ul

questions.question: The magnitude of buoyant force depends on the _________ of the fluid.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**density**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **Buoyant force** is the upward force exerted by a fluid on an object submerged in it. This force enables objects to float or rise in fluids.

• The magnitude of buoyant force depends on the **density of the fluid**. Higher fluid density results in a greater buoyant force.

• According to **Archimedes' principle**, the buoyant force is equal to the weight of the displaced fluid. The weight of the displaced fluid is determined by its density and volume.

• The formula for buoyant force is: **Fb = ρ × V × g**, where **ρ** is the density of the fluid, **V** is the volume of displaced fluid, and **g** is the acceleration due to gravity.

• Other properties like **refractive index**, **colour**, or **charge** do not influence buoyant force. These are unrelated to the physical interaction between the object and fluid.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Archimedes' Principle:** 

• It states that any object fully or partially submerged in a fluid experiences a buoyant force equal to the weight of the displaced fluid.

• This principle is applicable to both liquids and gases.

• It was discovered by the Greek mathematician and inventor **Archimedes** around 250 BC.

• **Density:**

• Density is defined as mass per unit volume: **ρ = m/V**.

• Units of density are typically expressed in **kg/m³** or **g/cm³**.

• Examples: Water has a density of **1000 kg/m³**, while air has a density of approximately **1.225 kg/m³** at sea level.

• **Applications of Buoyant Force:**

• **Shipbuilding:** Large ships float because their design ensures the weight of displaced water is greater than the weight of the ship.

• **Submarines:** Submarines adjust their buoyancy by controlling water and air in ballast tanks.

• **Hot Air Balloons:** The buoyant force from the surrounding cooler air lifts the balloon filled with heated air.

• **Factors Affecting Buoyant Force:**

• **Density of Fluid:** Higher density fluids exert greater buoyant force.

• **Volume of Object Submerged:** Larger submerged volume displaces more fluid and increases buoyant force.

• **Gravitational Acceleration:** Variations in gravity influence buoyant force magnitude (e.g., weaker gravity on the Moon).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Refractive Index:** 

• This property measures how much light bends when it enters a material. It has no connection to buoyant force.

• **Colour:** 

• Colour is a visual property determined by the wavelength of light reflected by an object or fluid. It does not affect buoyancy.

• **Charge:** 

• Charge refers to the electrical property of particles. It does not interact with buoyant force, which is a mechanical phenomenon.

questions.question: Personal Disposable Income is the part of the aggregate income which belongs to the ________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**households**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **Personal Disposable Income (PDI)** refers to the portion of aggregate income that remains with **households** after accounting for taxes and mandatory contributions, such as social security payments.

• This income is available for households to spend on **consumption** (goods and services) or to save for future needs.

• PDI is calculated by subtracting **personal taxes (e.g., income tax)** and non-tax payments (e.g., fines) from **personal income**.

• The primary recipients of Personal Disposable Income are **households**, as they are the economic units responsible for consumption and savings in an economy.

• It is a key indicator in macroeconomics used to measure the **financial health of households** and their ability to contribute to economic growth through spending and saving.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Key Components of Personal Income:**

• **Wages and Salaries:** Earnings from employment form a significant part of personal income.

• **Investment Income:** This includes interest, dividends, and rental income.

• **Government Transfers:** Payments like pensions, unemployment benefits, and subsidies.

• **Calculation of Personal Disposable Income:**

• Formula: **PDI = Personal Income - Taxes - Non-Tax Payments.**

• It excludes corporate taxes and retains only the income attributed to households.

• **Significance of PDI:**

• It is a direct measure of the **purchasing power** of households.

• Higher disposable income leads to increased **consumer spending**, boosting economic growth.

• It is also used to calculate the **Personal Savings Rate (PSR)**, which is a measure of household savings as a percentage of disposable income.

• **Difference from Other Income Metrics:**

• **National Income:** Measures total income generated by an economy, including businesses and government.

• **Gross Domestic Product (GDP):** The total market value of all goods and services produced in a country.

• **Personal Income:** Includes all income received by individuals, before taxes and other deductions.

• **Examples of Usage:**

• A household earning $50,000 annually, paying $10,000 in taxes, has a disposable income of **$40,000.**

• In policy-making, governments use PDI data to design tax policies or assess the impact of fiscal decisions on households.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Households:** Represent the **basic consumption units** in an economy. They are the primary recipients of disposable income and are responsible for economic activities like spending and saving.

• **Firms:** These are production units in the economy. They generate income through business activities but are not recipients of disposable income.

• **Government:** Collects taxes and provides transfers but does not retain disposable income for consumption.

• **Foreign Banks:** Operate in an economy to manage finances but do not directly relate to the concept of disposable income.
</ul

questions.question: In India, projects having a minimum investment of Rs. ________ Crore in plant & machinery shall be considered for establishment as EOUs.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In India, the **Export Oriented Units (EOUs)** scheme was introduced to promote export production and increase foreign exchange earnings by focusing on manufacturing goods solely for export purposes.
 
• EOUs are governed by the provisions of the **Foreign Trade Policy**, and they are eligible for various incentives and exemptions to boost their export capabilities.
 
• Projects with a minimum investment of **Rs. 1 Crore** in plant and machinery are considered eligible for establishment as EOUs. This ensures that only projects with substantial investment and operational capacity are approved.
 
• The investment threshold of Rs. 10 Crore ensures that EOUs are capable of contributing significantly to exports and foreign exchange reserves of the country.
 
• This criterion aligns with the government's vision to promote industrial development and global trade competitiveness by enabling large-scale production units to operate efficiently.
 
• *Hence, option 2 is correct.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Export Oriented Units (EOUs):**

 
 
• EOUs are set up with the primary purpose of producing goods exclusively for export.
 
• They are granted tax exemptions and duty-free import benefits for raw materials, components, and machinery required for production.
 
• EOUs function under the **Special Economic Zones (SEZs) Act, 2005**, with the aim of promoting export-centric industrialization.
 
• These units can be established in manufacturing, agriculture, aquaculture, and other sectors contributing to exports.
 
 
 
• **Government Incentives for EOUs:**
 
 
• EOUs enjoy benefits such as exemption from customs duty, excise duty, and Goods and Services Tax (**GST**) on inputs used in manufacturing goods for export.
 
• They are also provided with relaxation in foreign exchange regulations under the **Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA).**
 
• The central government provides **single-window clearance** to expedite approvals and facilitate smooth operations for EOUs.
 
 
 
• **Minimum Investment Threshold:**
 
 
• The threshold of **Rs. 1 Crore** in plant and machinery ensures that EOUs have the necessary infrastructure to produce high-quality goods for export.
 
• This eligibility criterion is designed to enable large-scale production capabilities and meet international standards.
 
 
 
• **Impact of EOUs:**
 
 
• EOUs contribute significantly to India's **GDP**, foreign exchange reserves, and employment generation.
 
• They enhance India's global competitiveness by ensuring adherence to international quality standards.
 
• Examples of successful EOUs include sectors like **IT services, textiles, pharmaceuticals, and electronics manufacturing.**
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Foreign Trade Policy:**

 
 
• The **Foreign Trade Policy (FTP)**, issued by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, provides guidelines for promoting exports through EOUs and other schemes.
 
• The FTP outlines the operational framework, incentives, and compliance requirements for EOUs.
 
 
 
• **SEZs vs EOUs:**
 
 
• While EOUs primarily focus on manufacturing goods for export, **Special Economic Zones (SEZs)** offer a broader scope, including services and trade activities.
 
• Both EOUs and SEZs aim to enhance India's export-oriented industrial development, but EOUs are specifically dedicated to manufacturing.
 
 
 
• **Investment and Growth:**
 
 
• The Rs. 10 Crore investment threshold encourages large-scale industrial growth and export competitiveness.
 
• This policy helps attract foreign direct investment (**FDI**) and strengthens India's trade relations globally.

questions.question: A Bill passed by the Indian State Legislature is sent to the Governor under _______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 200**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 200** of the **Indian Constitution** empowers the **Governor of a state** to grant assent, withhold assent, or reserve a bill for the consideration of the **President of India**.
 
• When a bill is passed by the **State Legislature**, it is sent to the Governor for approval. The Governor can exercise four options: **grant assent**, **withhold assent**, **return the bill** for reconsideration, or **reserve the bill** for the President’s consideration.
 
• If the Governor reserves the bill for consideration by the **President**, the President may grant assent, withhold assent, or suggest amendments to the bill.
 
• This power ensures that the provisions in the bill align with the **Constitution** and do not conflict with central laws or policies.
 
• **Article 200** thus plays a critical role in maintaining the balance between state and central legislative processes.
 
• ***Hence, Article 200 is the correct answer.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Article 201:**

 
 
• **Article 201** deals with the procedure when a bill reserved by the Governor for the **President’s consideration** is returned with or without recommendations.
 
• The President may suggest amendments to the bill or withhold approval, ensuring checks and balances in legislative matters.
 
 
 
• **Article 202:**
 
 
• **Article 202** pertains to the **annual financial statement** (budget) presented to the State Legislature by the Governor.
 
• This article ensures proper financial management and accountability within the state.
 
 
 
• **Article 203:**
 
 
• **Article 203** deals with the procedure for discussing the **appropriation and finance bills** in the State Legislature.
 
• It allows the legislature to examine, amend, and approve financial proposals for the state.
 
 
 
• **Governor's Role:**
 
 
• The **Governor** is a constitutional authority appointed by the **President of India** to act as the head of a state.
 
• The Governor's responsibilities include granting assent to bills, summoning the legislature, and overseeing state governance.
 
• The Governor also acts as a bridge between the **State Legislature** and the **Central Government**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Constitutional Context:**

 
 
• The **Indian Constitution** provides a framework to ensure coordination between the state and central legislative processes.
 
• Articles related to the Governor’s powers (200-203) highlight the role of the Governor in maintaining legislative integrity and constitutional compliance.
 
 
 
• **Checks and Balances:**
 
 
• By reserving bills for the President, the Governor ensures that state laws do not conflict with central laws or policies.
 
• This mechanism prevents misuse of legislative powers and maintains harmony between different levels of government.

questions.question:
When do desert plants typically take up carbon dioxide?

I. During the day

II. During the night
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**During the night**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• Desert plants primarily take up **carbon dioxide (CO₂) during the night** through a unique adaptation called **Crassulacean Acid Metabolism (CAM)**. This helps them conserve water in arid environments. 
• During the night, stomata (small pores on leaves) open to absorb CO₂, which is stored as an organic acid. This process minimizes water loss since temperatures are cooler and humidity is higher at night. 
• During the day, the stomata remain closed to prevent water loss, and the stored organic acids are broken down to release CO₂ for photosynthesis. This ensures efficient water use. 
• This adaptation is particularly important in deserts, where water is scarce, and high daytime temperatures can lead to excessive water loss through transpiration. 
• Hence, the statement "During the night" is correct, while "During the day" is incorrect as desert plants do not open their stomata during the hot daytime to avoid water loss. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Crassulacean Acid Metabolism (CAM):** 
• CAM is a specialized photosynthetic pathway that enables plants to open their stomata at night to take in CO₂ and store it as organic acids. 
• During the day, the stomata close, and the stored organic acids release CO₂ for photosynthesis. 
• CAM is common in desert plants like **cacti, agave, and succulents**, as well as epiphytes. 
• **Desert Plant Adaptations:** 
• To survive in arid conditions, desert plants exhibit adaptations like waxy leaf coatings, reduced leaf size, and deep root systems. 
• These adaptations minimize water loss and maximize water uptake. 
• **Stomatal Function:** 
• Stomata are tiny pores found on the surface of leaves, responsible for gas exchange. 
• In desert plants, stomata open at night to conserve water, unlike most plants that open stomata during the day. 
• **Examples of CAM Plants:** 
• **Cacti:** Adapted to extreme arid conditions, storing water in their stems and performing CAM photosynthesis. 
• **Agave:** Used for producing tequila and is highly drought-resistant. 
• **Succulents:** Store water in their leaves and thrive in dry climates. 
• **Importance of CAM Photosynthesis:** 
• Allows plants to grow in environments with limited water availability. 
• Helps maintain ecological balance in desert ecosystems. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Water Efficiency:** CAM plants use water up to **5-10 times more efficiently** than plants using C3 or C4 photosynthesis. 
• **Global Distribution:** CAM photosynthesis is not limited to deserts but is also found in tropical and subtropical areas. 
• **Ecological Role:** CAM plants contribute to stabilizing soil in arid regions, preventing erosion, and supporting desert fauna. 
• **Economic Importance:** Many CAM plants, such as **pineapple and agave**, have significant agricultural and commercial value. </ul

questions.question: Which of the following part of brain is responsible for the precision of voluntary actions and maintaining the posture and balance of the body?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Cerebellum**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• The **Cerebellum** is a part of the hindbrain that plays a critical role in coordinating **voluntary actions**, ensuring precision and smoothness of movements. 
• It is responsible for maintaining the body's **posture and balance**, allowing individuals to perform tasks such as walking, running, or standing upright. 
• The cerebellum processes sensory inputs from muscles, joints, and inner ear structures (vestibular system) to ensure proper motor control and coordination. 
• It also helps in fine-tuning motor activities like writing, typing, or playing musical instruments by regulating muscle movements. 
• Damage to the cerebellum can result in motor disorders such as **ataxia**, characterized by uncoordinated movements and difficulty maintaining balance. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Cerebrum:** 
• The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain and is associated with higher cognitive functions such as **thinking, memory, reasoning, and problem-solving**. 
• It is divided into two hemispheres, each responsible for controlling the opposite side of the body. 
• It also governs sensory perception and voluntary muscle movements but does not specialize in precision or balance. 
• **Medulla:** 
• The medulla, part of the brainstem, is primarily responsible for controlling **involuntary functions** such as breathing, heart rate, and blood pressure. 
• While vital for survival, it does not play a direct role in coordinating voluntary movements or maintaining body balance. 
• **Hypothalamus:** 
• The hypothalamus is a small but crucial part of the brain that regulates **homeostasis**, including body temperature, hunger, thirst, and hormonal balance. 
• It is involved in emotional responses and the endocrine system but does not contribute to motor coordination or posture. 
• **Function of Cerebellum:** 
• The cerebellum integrates sensory information from the **vestibular apparatus** (inner ear), visual signals, and proprioceptors (muscle/joint sensors). 
• It ensures smooth and accurate execution of motor activities, critical for tasks requiring precision, such as sports, dance, or surgical procedures. 
• It is located at the back of the brain, below the cerebrum, and connects with the spinal cord and other brain structures. 
• Modern research indicates its role in cognitive functions like attention and language in addition to motor skills. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Evolutionary Perspective:** The cerebellum is evolutionarily ancient and is present in most vertebrates, highlighting its importance in motor control. 
• **Clinical Application:** Damage to the cerebellum is assessed through tests like finger-to-nose coordination and heel-to-shin tests in neurological evaluations. 
• **Neuroplasticity:** The cerebellum exhibits neuroplasticity, meaning it can adapt and reorganize functions after injury, emphasizing its dynamic role in motor learning. </ul

questions.question: Samudragupta celebrated his conquests by performing which Vedic sacrifice?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ashvamedha**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

• **Samudragupta**, one of the greatest rulers of the **Gupta Empire**, celebrated his conquests by performing the **Ashvamedha Yajna**, a significant Vedic ritual.

• The **Ashvamedha Yajna** symbolized the authority and sovereignty of the emperor over his territories and neighboring regions.

• In this ritual, a sacred horse was allowed to roam freely across the kingdom and neighboring areas. Any territory where the horse was not challenged became a part of the ruler's domain.

• The performance of the Ashvamedha sacrifice was a mark of **political supremacy**, showcasing Samudragupta's consolidation of power and vast territorial expansion.

• The **Allahabad Pillar Inscription**, composed by Harisena, highlights Samudragupta's achievements and references the Ashvamedha sac
